class="tsingle" style="width:139px;max-width:139px"><div class="thumbimage" style="height:194px;overflow:hidden"><span typeof="mw:File"><a href="/wiki/File:Lesya_Ukrainka_portrait.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d5/Lesya_Ukrainka_portrait.jpg/137px-Lesya_Ukrainka_portrait.jpg" decoding="async" width="137" height="218" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d5/Lesya_Ukrainka_portrait.jpg/206px-Lesya_Ukrainka_portrait.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d5/Lesya_Ukrainka_portrait.jpg/274px-Lesya_Ukrainka_portrait.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1297" data-file-height="2061" /></a></span></div><div class="thumbcaption"><a href="/wiki/Lesya_Ukrainka" title="Lesya Ukrainka">Lesya Ukrainka</a>, one of the foremost Ukrainian women writers</div></div></div></div></div>
<p>The <a href="/wiki/Cossacks" title="Cossacks">Cossacks</a> established an independent society and popularized a <a href="/wiki/Duma_(epic)" title="Duma (epic)">new kind</a> of <a href="/wiki/Epic_poetry" title="Epic poetry">epic poem</a>, which marked a high point of Ukrainian <a href="/wiki/Oral_literature" title="Oral literature">oral literature</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-ualitmsn_385-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-ualitmsn-385">&#91;380&#93;</a></sup><sup class="noprint Inline-Template" style="white-space:nowrap;">&#91;<i><a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability" title="Wikipedia:Verifiability"><span title="The material near this tag failed verification of its source citation(s). (December 2022)">failed verification</span></a></i>&#93;</sup> These advances were then set back in the 17th and early 18th&#160;centuries, as many Ukrainian authors wrote in Russian or Polish. Nonetheless, by the late 18th&#160;century, the modern literary Ukrainian language finally emerged.<sup id="cite_ref-ualit_384-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-ualit-384">&#91;379&#93;</a></sup> In 1798, the modern era of the Ukrainian literary tradition began with <a href="/wiki/Ivan_Kotlyarevsky" class="mw-redirect" title="Ivan Kotlyarevsky">Ivan Kotlyarevsky</a>'s publication of <a href="/wiki/Eneida" title="Eneida">Eneida</a> in the Ukrainian vernacular.<sup id="cite_ref-387" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-387">&#91;381&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>By the 1830s, a Ukrainian <a href="/wiki/Romanticism" title="Romanticism">romantic literature</a> began to develop, and the nation's most renowned cultural figure, romanticist poet-painter <a href="/wiki/Taras_Shevchenko" title="Taras Shevchenko">Taras Shevchenko</a> emerged. Whereas Ivan Kotliarevsky is considered to be the father of literature in the Ukrainian vernacular; Shevchenko is the father of a national revival.<sup id="cite_ref-388" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-388">&#91;382&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Then, in 1863, the use of the Ukrainian language in print was effectively <a href="/wiki/Ems_Ukaz" title="Ems Ukaz">prohibited</a> by the Russian Empire.<sup id="cite_ref-censor_74-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-censor-74">&#91;71&#93;</a></sup> This severely curtailed literary activity in the area, and Ukrainian writers were forced to either publish their works in Russian or release them in Austrian controlled <a href="/wiki/Galicia_(Central_Europe)" class="mw-redirect" title="Galicia (Central Europe)">Galicia</a>. The ban was never officially lifted, but it became obsolete after the revolution and the Bolsheviks' coming to power.<sup id="cite_ref-ualitmsn_385-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-ualitmsn-385">&#91;380&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Ukrainian literature continued to flourish in the early Soviet years when nearly all literary trends were approved. These policies faced a steep decline in the 1930s, when prominent representatives as well as many others were killed by the <a href="/wiki/NKVD" title="NKVD">NKVD</a> during the <a href="/wiki/Great_Purge" title="Great Purge">Great Purge</a>. In general around 223 writers were repressed by what was known as the <a href="/wiki/Executed_Renaissance" title="Executed Renaissance">Executed Renaissance</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-389" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-389">&#91;383&#93;</a></sup> These repressions were part of Stalin's implemented policy of <a href="/wiki/Socialist_realism" title="Socialist realism">socialist realism</a>. The doctrine did not necessarily repress the use of the Ukrainian language, but it required that writers follow a certain style in their works.
</p><p>Literary freedom grew in the late 1980s and early 1990s alongside the decline and collapse of the USSR and the reestablishment of Ukrainian independence in 1991.<sup id="cite_ref-ualit_384-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-ualit-384">&#91;379&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Architecture">Architecture</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Ukrainian_architecture" title="Ukrainian architecture">Ukrainian architecture</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:80-391-9007_Kyiv_St.Michael%27s_Golden-Domed_Monastery_RB_18.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9b/80-391-9007_Kyiv_St.Michael%27s_Golden-Domed_Monastery_RB_18.jpg/220px-80-391-9007_Kyiv_St.Michael%27s_Golden-Domed_Monastery_RB_18.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="147" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9b/80-391-9007_Kyiv_St.Michael%27s_Golden-Domed_Monastery_RB_18.jpg/330px-80-391-9007_Kyiv_St.Michael%27s_Golden-Domed_Monastery_RB_18.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9b/80-391-9007_Kyiv_St.Michael%27s_Golden-Domed_Monastery_RB_18.jpg/440px-80-391-9007_Kyiv_St.Michael%27s_Golden-Domed_Monastery_RB_18.jpg 2x" data-file-width="5400" data-file-height="3600" /></a><figcaption><a href="/wiki/St._Michael%27s_Golden-Domed_Monastery" title="St. Michael&#39;s Golden-Domed Monastery">St Michael's Golden-domed Cathedral</a> in <a href="/wiki/Kyiv" title="Kyiv">Kyiv</a>, the foremost example of <a href="/wiki/Cossack_Baroque" class="mw-redirect" title="Cossack Baroque">Cossack Baroque</a> and one of Ukraine's most recognizable landmarks</figcaption></figure>
<p>Ukrainian architecture includes the motifs and styles that are found in structures built in modern Ukraine, and by <a href="/wiki/Ukrainians" title="Ukrainians">Ukrainians</a> worldwide. These include initial roots which were established in the state of <a href="/wiki/Kievan_Rus%27" title="Kievan Rus&#39;">Kievan Rus'</a>. Following the <a href="/wiki/Christianization_of_Kievan_Rus%27" title="Christianization of Kievan Rus&#39;">Christianization of Kievan Rus'</a>, Ukrainian architecture has been influenced by <a href="/wiki/Byzantine_architecture" title="Byzantine architecture">Byzantine architecture</a>. After the <a href="/wiki/Mongol_invasion_of_Kievan_Rus%27" title="Mongol invasion of Kievan Rus&#39;">Mongol invasion of Kievan Rus'</a>, it continued to develop in the <a href="/wiki/Kingdom_of_Galicia-Volhynia" class="mw-redirect" title="Kingdom of Galicia-Volhynia">Kingdom of Galicia-Volhynia</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-KatchanovskiKohutNebesio2013_390-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-KatchanovskiKohutNebesio2013-390">&#91;384&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>After the union with the <a href="/wiki/Tsardom_of_Russia" title="Tsardom of Russia">Tsardom of Russia</a>, architecture in Ukraine began to develop in different directions, with many structures in the larger eastern, Russian-ruled area built in the styles of <a href="/wiki/Russian_architecture" class="mw-redirect" title="Russian architecture">Russian architecture</a> of that period, whilst the western region of <a href="/wiki/Galicia_(Central_Europe)" class="mw-redirect" title="Galicia (Central Europe)">Galicia</a> developed under <a href="/wiki/Architecture_of_Poland" title="Architecture of Poland">Polish</a> and <a href="/wiki/Architecture_of_Austria" class="mw-redirect" title="Architecture of Austria">Austro-Hungarian architectural influences</a>. Ukrainian national motifs would eventually be used during the period of the <a href="/wiki/Soviet_Union" title="Soviet Union">Soviet Union</a> and in modern independent Ukraine.<sup id="cite_ref-KatchanovskiKohutNebesio2013_390-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-KatchanovskiKohutNebesio2013-390">&#91;384&#93;</a></sup> However, much of the contemporary architectural skyline of Ukraine is dominated by Soviet-style <a href="/wiki/Khrushchyovka" class="mw-redirect" title="Khrushchyovka">Khrushchyovkas</a>, or low-cost apartment buildings.<sup id="cite_ref-391" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-391">&#91;385&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Weaving_and_embroidery">Weaving and embroidery</span></h3>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Rushnyk_Ukraine_embroidered_decorative_towels.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/10/Rushnyk_Ukraine_embroidered_decorative_towels.jpg/170px-Rushnyk_Ukraine_embroidered_decorative_towels.jpg" decoding="async" width="170" height="188" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/10/Rushnyk_Ukraine_embroidered_decorative_towels.jpg/255px-Rushnyk_Ukraine_embroidered_decorative_towels.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/10/Rushnyk_Ukraine_embroidered_decorative_towels.jpg/340px-Rushnyk_Ukraine_embroidered_decorative_towels.jpg 2x" data-file-width="768" data-file-height="848" /></a><figcaption><a href="/wiki/Rushnyk" title="Rushnyk">Rushnyk</a>, <a href="/wiki/Ukrainian_embroidery" title="Ukrainian embroidery">Ukrainian embroidery</a></figcaption></figure>
<p>Artisan <a href="/wiki/Textile_arts" title="Textile arts">textile arts</a> play an important role in Ukrainian culture,<sup id="cite_ref-392" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-392">&#91;386&#93;</a></sup> especially in <a href="/wiki/Ukrainian_wedding_traditions" title="Ukrainian wedding traditions">Ukrainian wedding traditions</a>. <a href="/wiki/Ukrainian_embroidery" title="Ukrainian embroidery">Ukrainian embroidery</a>, <a href="/wiki/Weaving" title="Weaving">weaving</a> and lace-making are used in traditional <a href="/wiki/Folk_dress" class="mw-redirect" title="Folk dress">folk dress</a> and in traditional celebrations. Ukrainian embroidery varies depending on the region of origin<sup id="cite_ref-393" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-393">&#91;387&#93;</a></sup> and the designs have a long history of motifs, compositions, choice of colours and types of stitches.<sup id="cite_ref-museum_394-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-museum-394">&#91;388&#93;</a></sup> Use of colour is very important and has roots in <a href="/wiki/Ukrainian_folklore" title="Ukrainian folklore">Ukrainian folklore</a>. Embroidery motifs found in different parts of Ukraine are preserved in the <a href="/wiki/Rushnyk" title="Rushnyk">Rushnyk</a> Museum in <a href="/wiki/Pereiaslav" title="Pereiaslav">Pereiaslav</a>.
</p><p>National dress is woven and highly decorated. Weaving with handmade looms is still practised in the village of Krupove, situated in <a href="/wiki/Rivne_Oblast" title="Rivne Oblast">Rivne Oblast</a>. The village is the birthplace of two internationally recognized personalities in the scene of national crafts fabrication: Nina Myhailivna<sup id="cite_ref-395" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-395">&#91;389&#93;</a></sup> and Uliana Petrivna.<sup id="cite_ref-396" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-396">&#91;390&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Music">Music</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Music_of_Ukraine" title="Music of Ukraine">Music of Ukraine</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Fedir_Stovbynenko_-_Kozak-bandyryst_(1890).jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c4/Fedir_Stovbynenko_-_Kozak-bandyryst_%281890%29.jpg/170px-Fedir_Stovbynenko_-_Kozak-bandyryst_%281890%29.jpg" decoding="async" width="170" height="182" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c4/Fedir_Stovbynenko_-_Kozak-bandyryst_%281890%29.jpg/255px-Fedir_Stovbynenko_-_Kozak-bandyryst_%281890%29.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c4/Fedir_Stovbynenko_-_Kozak-bandyryst_%281890%29.jpg/340px-Fedir_Stovbynenko_-_Kozak-bandyryst_%281890%29.jpg 2x" data-file-width="998" data-file-height="1068" /></a><figcaption><a href="/wiki/Cossack_Mamay" title="Cossack Mamay">Cossack Mamay</a> playing a <a href="/wiki/Kobza" title="Kobza">kobza</a></figcaption></figure>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:%D0%9B%D0%B8%D1%81%D0%B5%D0%BD%D0%BA%D0%BE_%D0%9C%D0%B8%D0%BA%D0%BE%D0%BB%D0%B0_(cropped).jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d9/%D0%9B%D0%B8%D1%81%D0%B5%D0%BD%D0%BA%D0%BE_%D0%9C%D0%B8%D0%BA%D0%BE%D0%BB%D0%B0_%28cropped%29.jpg/170px-%D0%9B%D0%B8%D1%81%D0%B5%D0%BD%D0%BA%D0%BE_%D0%9C%D0%B8%D0%BA%D0%BE%D0%BB%D0%B0_%28cropped%29.jpg" decoding="async" width="170" height="222" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d9/%D0%9B%D0%B8%D1%81%D0%B5%D0%BD%D0%BA%D0%BE_%D0%9C%D0%B8%D0%BA%D0%BE%D0%BB%D0%B0_%28cropped%29.jpg/255px-%D0%9B%D0%B8%D1%81%D0%B5%D0%BD%D0%BA%D0%BE_%D0%9C%D0%B8%D0%BA%D0%BE%D0%BB%D0%B0_%28cropped%29.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d9/%D0%9B%D0%B8%D1%81%D0%B5%D0%BD%D0%BA%D0%BE_%D0%9C%D0%B8%D0%BA%D0%BE%D0%BB%D0%B0_%28cropped%29.jpg/340px-%D0%9B%D0%B8%D1%81%D0%B5%D0%BD%D0%BA%D0%BE_%D0%9C%D0%B8%D0%BA%D0%BE%D0%BB%D0%B0_%28cropped%29.jpg 2x" data-file-width="377" data-file-height="493" /></a><figcaption><a href="/wiki/Mykola_Lysenko" title="Mykola Lysenko">Mykola Lysenko</a> is widely considered to be the father of Ukrainian classical music.<sup id="cite_ref-Risch_2011_p._44_397-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Risch_2011_p._44-397">&#91;391&#93;</a></sup></figcaption></figure>
<p>Music is a major part of Ukrainian culture, with a long history and many influences. From traditional <a href="/wiki/Folk_music" title="Folk music">folk music</a>, to <a href="/wiki/Classical_music" title="Classical music">classical</a> and <a href="/wiki/Modern_rock" title="Modern rock">modern rock</a>, Ukraine has produced several internationally recognised musicians including <a href="/wiki/Kirill_Karabits" title="Kirill Karabits">Kirill Karabits</a>, <a href="/wiki/Okean_Elzy" title="Okean Elzy">Okean Elzy</a> and <a href="/wiki/Ruslana" title="Ruslana">Ruslana</a>. Elements from traditional Ukrainian folk music made their way into Western music and even into modern <a href="/wiki/Jazz" title="Jazz">jazz</a>. Ukrainian music sometimes presents a perplexing mix of exotic melismatic singing with chordal harmony. The most striking general characteristic of authentic ethnic Ukrainian folk music is the wide use of minor modes or keys which incorporate augmented second intervals.<sup id="cite_ref-Sonevytsky_2019_p._398-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Sonevytsky_2019_p.-398">&#91;392&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>During the Baroque period, music had a place of considerable importance in the curriculum of the <a href="/wiki/Kyiv-Mohyla_Academy" class="mw-redirect" title="Kyiv-Mohyla Academy">Kyiv-Mohyla Academy</a>. Much of the nobility was well versed in music with many Ukrainian Cossack leaders such as (<a href="/wiki/Ivan_Mazepa" title="Ivan Mazepa">Mazepa</a>, <a href="/wiki/Semen_Paliy" title="Semen Paliy">Paliy</a>, <a href="/wiki/Antin_Holovaty" title="Antin Holovaty">Holovatyj</a>, <a href="/wiki/Ivan_Sirko" title="Ivan Sirko">Sirko</a>) being accomplished players of the <a href="/wiki/Kobza" title="Kobza">kobza</a>, <a href="/wiki/Bandura" title="Bandura">bandura</a> or <a href="/wiki/Torban" title="Torban">torban</a>.
</p><p>The first dedicated musical academy was set up in <a href="/wiki/Hlukhiv" title="Hlukhiv">Hlukhiv</a> in 1738 and students were taught to sing and play violin and bandura from manuscripts. As a result, many of the earliest composers and performers within the Russian empire were ethnically Ukrainian, having been born or educated in Hlukhiv or having been closely associated with this music school.<sup id="cite_ref-Struk_1993_p._1461_399-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Struk_1993_p._1461-399">&#91;393&#93;</a></sup> Ukrainian classical music differs considerably depending on whether the composer was of Ukrainian ethnicity living in Ukraine, a composer of non-Ukrainian ethnicity who was a citizen of Ukraine, or part of the <a href="/wiki/Ukrainian_diaspora" title="Ukrainian diaspora">Ukrainian diaspora</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-Ukrainian_people_2017_400-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Ukrainian_people_2017-400">&#91;394&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Since the mid-1960s, Western-influenced pop music has been growing in popularity in Ukraine. Folk singer and harmonium player <a href="/wiki/Mariana_Sadovska" title="Mariana Sadovska">Mariana Sadovska</a> is prominent. Ukrainian pop and folk music arose with the international popularity of groups and performers like <a href="/wiki/Vopli_Vidoplyasova" class="mw-redirect" title="Vopli Vidoplyasova">Vopli Vidoplyasova</a>, <a href="/wiki/Dakh_Daughters" title="Dakh Daughters">Dakh Daughters</a>, <a href="/wiki/Dakha_Brakha" class="mw-redirect" title="Dakha Brakha">Dakha Brakha</a>, <a href="/wiki/Ivan_Dorn" title="Ivan Dorn">Ivan Dorn</a> and <a href="/wiki/Okean_Elzy" title="Okean Elzy">Okean Elzy</a>.
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Media">Media</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Media_of_Ukraine" class="mw-redirect" title="Media of Ukraine">Media of Ukraine</a></div>
<p>The Ukrainian legal framework on media freedom is deemed "among the most progressive in eastern Europe", although implementation has been uneven.<sup id="cite_ref-FH_401-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FH-401">&#91;395&#93;</a></sup><sup class="noprint Inline-Template" style="white-space:nowrap;">&#91;<i><a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual_of_Style/Dates_and_numbers#Chronological_items" title="Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers"><span title="The date of the event predicted near this tag has passed. (December 2022)">needs update</span></a></i>&#93;</sup> The constitution and laws provide for <a href="/wiki/Freedom_of_speech" title="Freedom of speech">freedom of speech</a><sup id="cite_ref-402" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-402">&#91;396&#93;</a></sup> and <a href="/wiki/Freedom_of_the_press_in_Ukraine" title="Freedom of the press in Ukraine">press</a>. The main regulatory authority for the broadcast media is the <a href="/wiki/National_Television_and_Radio_Broadcasting_Council_of_Ukraine" class="mw-redirect" title="National Television and Radio Broadcasting Council of Ukraine">National Television and Radio Broadcasting Council of Ukraine</a> (NTRBCU), tasked with licensing media outlets and ensure their compliance with the law.<sup id="cite_ref-403" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-403">&#91;397&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p><a href="/wiki/Kyiv" title="Kyiv">Kyiv</a> dominates the media sector in Ukraine: National <a href="/wiki/List_of_newspapers_in_Ukraine" title="List of newspapers in Ukraine">newspapers</a> <i><a href="/wiki/Den_(newspaper)" class="mw-redirect" title="Den (newspaper)">Den</a></i>, <i><a href="/wiki/Dzerkalo_Tyzhnia" title="Dzerkalo Tyzhnia">Dzerkalo Tyzhnia</a></i>, tabloids, such as <i><a href="/wiki/The_Ukrainian_Week" title="The Ukrainian Week">The Ukrainian Week</a></i> or <i><a href="/wiki/Focus_(Ukrainian_magazine)" title="Focus (Ukrainian magazine)">Focus</a></i>, and television and radio are largely based there,<sup class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">&#91;<i><a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><span title="This claim needs references to reliable sources. (March 2022)">citation needed</span></a></i>&#93;</sup> although <a href="/wiki/Lviv" title="Lviv">Lviv</a> is also a significant national media centre. The National News Agency of Ukraine, <a href="/wiki/Ukrinform" title="Ukrinform">Ukrinform</a> was founded here in 1918. <a href="/wiki/BBC_Ukrainian" class="mw-redirect" title="BBC Ukrainian">BBC Ukrainian</a> started its broadcasts in 1992.<sup id="cite_ref-404" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-404">&#91;398&#93;</a></sup> As of 2022<sup class="plainlinks noexcerpt noprint asof-tag update" style="display:none;"><a class="external text" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ukraine&amp;action=edit">&#91;update&#93;</a></sup> 75% of the population use the internet, and social media is widely used by government and people.<sup id="cite_ref-405" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-405">&#91;399&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Sport">Sport</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Sport_in_Ukraine" title="Sport in Ukraine">Sport in Ukraine</a></div>
<p>Ukraine greatly benefited from the Soviet emphasis on <a href="/wiki/Physical_education" title="Physical education">physical education</a>. These policies left Ukraine with hundreds of stadia, swimming pools, gymnasia and many other athletic facilities.<sup id="cite_ref-406" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-406">&#91;400&#93;</a></sup> The most popular sport is <a href="/wiki/Association_football" title="Association football">football</a>. The top professional league is the <a href="/wiki/Ukrainian_Premier_League" title="Ukrainian Premier League">Vyscha Liha</a> ("premier league").
</p><p>Many Ukrainians also played for the <a href="/wiki/Soviet_national_football_team" class="mw-redirect" title="Soviet national football team">Soviet national football team</a>, most notably <a href="/wiki/Ballon_d%27Or" title="Ballon d&#39;Or">Ballon d'Or</a> winners <a href="/wiki/Ihor_Belanov" class="mw-redirect" title="Ihor Belanov">Ihor Belanov</a> and <a href="/wiki/Oleh_Blokhin" class="mw-redirect" title="Oleh Blokhin">Oleh Blokhin</a>. This award was only presented to one Ukrainian after the dissolution of the Soviet Union, <a href="/wiki/Andriy_Shevchenko" title="Andriy Shevchenko">Andriy Shevchenko</a>. The national team made its debut in the <a href="/wiki/2006_FIFA_World_Cup" title="2006 FIFA World Cup">2006 FIFA World Cup</a>, and reached the quarterfinals before losing to eventual champions, <a href="/wiki/Italy_national_football_team" title="Italy national football team">Italy</a>.
</p><p>Ukrainian <a href="/wiki/Boxing" title="Boxing">boxers</a> are amongst the best in the world.<sup id="cite_ref-407" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-407">&#91;401&#93;</a></sup> Since becoming the undisputed cruiserweight champion in 2018, <a href="/wiki/Oleksandr_Usyk" title="Oleksandr Usyk">Oleksandr Usyk</a> has also gone on to win the unified WBA (Super), IBF, WBO and IBO heavyweight titles. This feat made him one of only three boxers to have unified the cruiserweight world titles and become a world heavyweight champion.<sup id="cite_ref-408" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-408">&#91;402&#93;</a></sup> The brothers <a href="/wiki/Vitali_Klitschko" title="Vitali Klitschko">Vitali</a> and <a href="/wiki/Wladimir_Klitschko" title="Wladimir Klitschko">Wladimir Klitschko</a> are former <a href="/wiki/Heavyweight" title="Heavyweight">heavyweight</a> world champions who held multiple world titles throughout their careers. Also hailing from Ukraine is <a href="/wiki/Vasyl_Lomachenko" class="mw-redirect" title="Vasyl Lomachenko">Vasyl Lomachenko</a>, a <a href="/wiki/2008_Summer_Olympics" title="2008 Summer Olympics">2008</a> and <a href="/wiki/2012_Olympic_games" class="mw-redirect" title="2012 Olympic games">2012 Olympic</a> gold medalist. He is the <a href="/wiki/Unified_champion" class="mw-redirect" title="Unified champion">unified</a> <a href="/wiki/Lightweight" title="Lightweight">lightweight</a> world champion who ties the record for winning a world title in the fewest professional fights; three. As of September 2018, he is ranked as the world's best active boxer, <a href="/wiki/Pound_for_pound" title="Pound for pound">pound for pound</a>, by <a href="/wiki/Boxing_pound_for_pound_rankings#ESPN" title="Boxing pound for pound rankings">ESPN</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-409" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-409">&#91;403&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p><a href="/wiki/Sergey_Bubka" title="Sergey Bubka">Sergey Bubka</a> held the record in the <a href="/wiki/Pole_vault" title="Pole vault">Pole vault</a> from 1993 to 2014; with great strength, speed and gymnastic abilities, he was voted the world's best athlete on several occasions.<sup id="cite_ref-410" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-410">&#91;404&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-411" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-411">&#91;405&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p><a href="/wiki/Basketball" title="Basketball">Basketball</a> has gained popularity in Ukraine. In 2011, Ukraine was granted a right to organize <a href="/wiki/EuroBasket_2015" title="EuroBasket 2015">EuroBasket 2015</a>. Two years later the <a href="/wiki/Ukraine_national_basketball_team" class="mw-redirect" title="Ukraine national basketball team">Ukraine national basketball team</a> finished sixth in <a href="/wiki/EuroBasket_2013" title="EuroBasket 2013">EuroBasket 2013</a> and qualified to <a href="/wiki/2014_FIBA_Basketball_World_Cup" title="2014 FIBA Basketball World Cup">FIBA World Cup</a> for the first time in its history. <a href="/wiki/Euroleague" class="mw-redirect" title="Euroleague">Euroleague</a> participant <a href="/wiki/BC_Budivelnyk" title="BC Budivelnyk">Budivelnyk Kyiv</a> is the strongest professional basketball club in Ukraine.
</p><p><a href="/wiki/Chess" title="Chess">Chess</a> is a popular sport in Ukraine. <a href="/wiki/Ruslan_Ponomariov" title="Ruslan Ponomariov">Ruslan Ponomariov</a> is the former world champion. There are about 85 <a href="/wiki/Grandmaster_(chess)" title="Grandmaster (chess)">Grandmasters</a> and 198 <a href="/wiki/International_Masters" class="mw-redirect" title="International Masters">International Masters</a> in Ukraine. <a href="/wiki/Rugby_league" title="Rugby league">Rugby league</a> is played throughout Ukraine.<sup id="cite_ref-412" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-412">&#91;406&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Cuisine">Cuisine</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Ukrainian_cuisine" title="Ukrainian cuisine">Ukrainian cuisine</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Borscht_served.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a7/Borscht_served.jpg/220px-Borscht_served.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="144" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a7/Borscht_served.jpg/330px-Borscht_served.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a7/Borscht_served.jpg/440px-Borscht_served.jpg 2x" data-file-width="3636" data-file-height="2376" /></a><figcaption>Ukrainian <a href="/wiki/Borscht" title="Borscht">borscht</a> with <a href="/wiki/Smetana_(dairy_product)" title="Smetana (dairy product)">smetana</a> sour cream</figcaption></figure>
<p>The traditional Ukrainian diet includes chicken, pork, beef, fish and mushrooms. Ukrainians also tend to eat a lot of potatoes; grains; and fresh, boiled or pickled vegetables. Popular traditional dishes <i><span title="Ukrainian-language text"><i lang="uk-Latn"><a href="/wiki/Varenyky" class="mw-redirect" title="Varenyky">varenyky</a></i></span></i> (boiled dumplings with mushrooms, potatoes, <a href="/wiki/Sauerkraut" title="Sauerkraut">sauerkraut</a>, cottage cheese, cherries or berries), <i><a href="/wiki/Nalysnyky" class="mw-redirect" title="Nalysnyky">nalysnyky</a></i> (pancakes with cottage cheese, poppy seeds, mushrooms, <a href="/wiki/Caviar" title="Caviar">caviar</a> or meat), <i><a href="/wiki/Cabbage_soup" title="Cabbage soup">kapusnyak</a></i> (cabbage soup made with meat, potatoes, carrots, onions, millet, tomato paste, spices and fresh herbs), <a href="/wiki/Borscht" title="Borscht">borscht</a> (soup made of beets, cabbage and mushrooms or meat) and <span title="Ukrainian-language text"><i lang="uk-Latn"><a href="/wiki/Go%C5%82%C4%85bki" title="Gołąbki">holubtsy</a></i></span> (stuffed cabbage rolls filled with rice, carrots, onion and minced meat).<sup id="cite_ref-413" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-413">&#91;407&#93;</a></sup> Among traditional baked goods are decorated <a href="/wiki/Korovai" title="Korovai">korovais</a> and <a href="/wiki/Paska_(bread)" title="Paska (bread)">paska Easter bread</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-414" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-414">&#91;408&#93;</a></sup> Ukrainian specialties also include <a href="/wiki/Chicken_Kiev" title="Chicken Kiev">Chicken Kiev</a> and <a href="/wiki/Kyiv_cake" title="Kyiv cake">Kyiv cake</a>.
</p><p>Ukrainians drink <a href="/wiki/Kompot" title="Kompot">stewed fruit compote</a>, juices, milk, <a href="/wiki/Buttermilk" title="Buttermilk">buttermilk</a>, mineral water, tea and coffee, beer, wine and <span title="Ukrainian-language text"><i lang="uk-Latn"><a href="/wiki/Horilka" title="Horilka">horilka</a></i></span>.<sup id="cite_ref-415" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-415">&#91;409&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
